passage:
Anjali: So how did the history project go?
Wasim: Okay, don't laugh. It was due Friday at eight in the morning. On Thursday evening I still hadn't started the poster. And honestly, I felt fine. Around ten at night, the panic kicked in, and then something clicked. I was flying, cutting, gluing, writing captions in one long burst. I slept three hours. In the morning my hands were shaking and my eyes felt sandy, but I told myself, look, I can do it in one night. It felt like proof I was good. Then the teacher pointed out two wrong dates and a caption pasted upside down. I said “I know” and I didn't know what else to say. 😅

qa.q: At what time on Friday was the project due?
qa.a: The project was due on Friday at eight in the morning.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel after finishing the poster in one night?
qa.a: Wasim felt proud and excited, seeing it as proof of ability, though tired and shaky.

qa.q: What was the cost of the night-before rush?
qa.a: Wasim slept only three hours and handed in a poster with two wrong dates and an upside-down caption.

qa.q: How might Anjali react to hearing the story?
qa.a: Anjali is probably curious and sympathetic, and may notice that the feeling of proof came from pressure rather than from the poster's quality.

grounding: A teenager works frantically the night before a submission and delivers something rushed, taking the adrenaline as proof of ability.

passage: I'm Chaitanya. I live across the corridor from Vijay, and on Sunday night I saw Vijay's light on until nearly three. Through the door I could hear frantic typing, then a groan, then a whispered “no, no, no.” In the morning Vijay came out with red eyes, holding a printout, and said cheerfully, “Finished the whole report in one night. I work best like this.” It seemed a proud sentence, though I couldn't tell whether Vijay believed it or wished to. Later I heard the report came back with a comment about missing sections and a rushed conclusion. Vijay didn't mention the comment and asked if anyone had a spare pen.

qa.q: Until what time was Vijay's light on on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vijay's light was on until nearly three.

qa.q: What might Vijay have felt when saying “I work best like this”?
qa.a: Vijay may have been proud and relieved after the rush, yet perhaps also tired and hoping to believe it, but Chaitanya cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Vijay try before the next report to avoid a three a.m. finish?
qa.a: Start a few days earlier with a small piece each evening, so the final night is for checking, not creating.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya interpret Vijay's cheerful announcement?
qa.a: Chaitanya notices the pride but is not sure whether Vijay believes it, since the red eyes and the groans suggest a harder night.

grounding: A teenager works frantically the night before a submission and takes the adrenaline as proof of ability, seen by someone across the corridor.

passage: At eleven at night in the boarding-school hostel, Samir, sixteen, was still typing his physics lab report due at 8 a.m. The corridor lights were off; he worked by the glow of his laptop. Maria ma'am, the house warden, had done her last round at ten and told him to sleep soon. At two, Samir printed the pages in the common room, graphs slightly crooked. He felt a rush, almost pride. "I work best like this," he whispered to himself. At eight he submitted it, eyes burning. His teacher returned it a week later: "Good ideas, careless graphs, conclusion missing." Samir stared at the red ink and felt the rush drain out of him.

qa.q: When was Samir's physics lab report due?
qa.a: It was due at 8 a.m.

qa.q: What did Samir feel when he printed the pages at two?
qa.a: He felt a rush, almost pride, believing he works best under pressure.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The late-night rush left the graphs careless and the conclusion missing; starting a few days earlier would leave time to check.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Samir's report?
qa.a: The teacher sees good ideas spoiled by rushed work, and points out the careless graphs and missing conclusion.

grounding: Shows a teenager working frantically the night before, feeling the rush as proof of ability, and getting a rushed result.

passage:
Dear Sachin,

You asked how the geography project went. Honestly? I did the whole thing last night. Started at nine, finished at four in the morning. Maps, write-up, everything. And I felt amazing at three, like some kind of genius. The coffee, the silence, the panic, it all made me fast.

Then this morning I read it on the bus and saw I'd labelled the Ganga as the Yamuna. Twice. And half the write-up was one long paragraph. I got a C.

I keep telling myself I'm a pressure person. But maybe I only feel clever at 3 a.m. because I'm too tired to notice the mistakes.

Your cousin,
Hrithik

qa.q: What grade did Hrithik get on the geography project?
qa.a: Hrithik got a C.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel at three in the morning?
qa.a: Hrithik felt amazing, like a genius, fuelled by coffee, silence and panic.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try for the next project?
qa.a: Start a few days earlier and keep one calm evening to check the work, so errors like mixing up the rivers are caught.

qa.q: How might Sachin respond to this letter?
qa.a: Sachin might feel sympathetic and a little amused, and could encourage Hrithik to test starting earlier next time.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows working frantically the night before, feeling the adrenaline as ability, and delivering rushed work.

passage: Want to know my worst school habit? I'm Rajni, and in Class Eleven I lived for the night before. My friend Nandini would start projects a week early, and I'd tease her. "Where's the thrill?" The thrill for me was midnight: heart racing, fingers flying, the feeling that I could pull anything off. And I did pull things off, sort of. My biology file went in with smudged diagrams and a missing index. I slept three hours and fell asleep in the practical exam the next day. My teacher said, "You're capable, but I'm marking what's on the page." That line stayed with me. The rush felt like talent. The page said otherwise.

qa.q: How many hours did Rajni sleep before the practical exam?
qa.a: Rajni slept three hours.

qa.q: What did Rajni feel at midnight while working on projects?
qa.a: Rajni felt thrilled and excited, heart racing, sure of being able to pull anything off.

qa.q: What would you advise Rajni based on the teacher's comment?
qa.a: Start earlier like Nandini, so that the work on the page matches the ability, instead of relying on the midnight rush.

qa.q: How might Nandini have seen Rajni's teasing?
qa.a: Nandini may have found it mildly annoying but stayed calm, trusting her own early-start habit.

grounding: A teenager tells how the adrenaline of night-before work felt like ability but produced rushed, weaker results.

passage:
Monday: Mr Kulkarni handed out the economics case study, due Friday. "Plenty of time," Jagdish told Omkar in the canteen. "I work better at the last minute anyway."
Thursday night: At 11:40 the laptop was open, a bowl of instant noodles gone cold beside it. Jagdish typed fast, heart thumping, copying figures from the textbook table without checking them twice. The conclusion was three rushed lines. He printed it at 2:30 and slept three hours. On Friday he yawned through maths and snapped at his little sister at breakfast.
The following Monday: The file came back with a B-minus and a note in red: "Good ideas, weak conclusion, two figures wrong." Jagdish grinned at Omkar. "One night, bro. Imagine if I'd tried." Omkar looked at the red ink and said nothing.

qa.q: What time did Jagdish print the case study?
qa.a: He printed it at 2:30.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish grin on the following Monday?
qa.a: He felt proud and a bit thrilled that one frantic night had produced a passing grade, taking the rush as proof of his ability.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Leaving everything to Thursday night led to wrong figures, a weak conclusion and little sleep; starting on Monday or Tuesday would leave time to check the numbers and finish the conclusion.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the result differently?
qa.a: Omkar notices the red ink about the wrong figures and the weak conclusion, so Omkar may feel doubtful or quietly concerned rather than impressed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose night-before rush produces rushed work and little sleep, yet feels like proof of ability and strengthens the habit.
